periods.activity_title: Circle Definitions and Locating the Centre
materials: Circular cutouts of paper (one per student or pair)

time_bands.activity: Distribute circular paper cutouts. Ask students to fold the circle in half and crease, then fold again in a different direction and crease. Have them mark where the two creases meet. Pose the think-reflect question from Section 5.1: what method has Amina suggested for locating the centre, and why does folding work? Students share conjectures in pairs.

Formalise: a circle is the set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance (radius) from a fixed point (centre). Introduce radius, chord, and diameter, emphasising that a diameter is the longest chord and passes through the centre. Students label these on their own sketches, identifying at least two distinct chords and explaining why the diameter is a special chord.

Students derive, by measuring radii on their paper circles, that all points on the circle are equidistant from the centre. They write one sentence justifying Amina's folding method in terms of the definition: every fold crease through two circle-edge points is a chord; when it also passes through the centre it is a diameter. Each crease places the centre on the fold line, so the intersection of two creases is the centre.

Class discussion to consolidate: teacher draws a circle on the board, marks a chord that is not a diameter, and asks students to classify it. Students state the definition of each term aloud. Pose the closing question: how many diameters can a circle have, and what does that suggest about its symmetry? (Intentionally open — symmetry is taken up in the next section.)

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's circle vocabulary from the locus definition that unifies all subsequent theorems, so orient students to the idea that 'equidistant from a centre' is the precise claim underlying every result they will prove. A common error here is treating the word 'chord' as synonymous with 'diameter'; watch for students who assume all chords pass through the centre. Students who finish the folding task early may attempt Think and Reflect from Section 5.1 independently.
homework: Using a compass, draw a circle, mark its centre O, draw three distinct chords, and state which (if any) is a diameter. Measure all three lengths and list them in order.

periods.activity_title: Rotational and Reflection Symmetries of a Circle

time_bands.activity: Students fold a circular cutout along a diameter and observe that the two halves coincide. They repeat with a second and third diameter in different directions, recording each fold. Ask: how many such lines of reflection symmetry does a circle have? Students conjecture and share. The class agrees on 'infinitely many — one for each diameter' and students articulate why: folding along any diameter maps every point to a point equidistant from the centre on the opposite side.

Introduce rotational symmetry: fix the centre and rotate the circle by any angle; it maps onto itself. Ask the think-reflect questions from Section 5.2 — identify the rotational and reflection symmetries of a square, regular pentagon, and regular hexagon, then compare with a circle. Students record their answers: a square has 4-fold rotation and 4 reflection axes; a regular pentagon has 5-fold and 5 axes; a regular hexagon has 6-fold and 6 axes. The circle is the limiting case with infinitely many of each.

Ask: what is the longest chord? Students use the definition of radius and the triangle-inequality argument to confirm the diameter. Ask: what is the shortest possible chord? Guide students to see that a chord can shrink toward a single point (distance from centre approaching the radius), so there is no positive minimum — the 'smallest chord' question points toward the role of distance from the centre. Students also reason about the locus of points equidistant from two given points on the circle.

Wrap-up: each student writes two sentences — one describing why every diameter is a line of symmetry (using the equidistance definition), and one describing what complete rotational symmetry means for a circle. Collect to check for the common error below.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the definition of a circle in terms of equidistance from the centre, the symmetry results of this section follow naturally from that single property — help students see each symmetry as a consequence, not an additional assumption. A frequent error is conflating a line of symmetry with a diameter passing through a marked point rather than through the centre; make clear that every line of reflection symmetry must pass through the centre. The think-reflect on the locus of points equidistant from two given points anticipates the perpendicular-bisector result in Section 5.3.

periods.activity_title: How Many Circles Through Two or Three Points?

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the least possible radius of a circle through two given points A and B.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Think, Draw and Infer Q1, p.98
textbook_items_in_class.description: For three collinear points A, B, C, investigate whether a point P exists with PA = PB = PC; examine the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC, show they are parallel, and decide whether a circle can pass through collinear points or whether a line can cut a circle in three points.

time_bands.activity: Draw two points A and B on the board. Ask how many circles can pass through both. Students draw several examples with their compasses, quickly discovering many are possible. The teacher asks: where must each centre be? Students measure and find the centre always lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. Formalise: all centres of circles through A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB, giving infinitely many circles.

Pose Exercise Set 5.1 Q4, p.98: what is the smallest possible radius of such a circle? Students reason: the perpendicular bisector is a locus; the closest point on it to both A and B is the midpoint of AB, giving radius = AB/2. Confirm with a compass construction. The think-reflect questions on curvature along the perpendicular bisector and on how many squares can be drawn are discussed briefly as qualitative reasoning.

Extend to three non-collinear points. Students draw three points, construct perpendicular bisectors of two sides, find their intersection, and draw the circumscribed circle. Teacher leads the deductive proof of Theorem 1: the perpendicular bisectors of any two sides of a triangle meet at a unique point equidistant from all three vertices, which is the circumcentre. Locate the circumcentre for acute, obtuse, and right triangles (inside, outside, on the hypotenuse respectively).

Students work on Think, Draw and Infer Q1, p.98 (three collinear points). They show the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC are parallel, so no circumcentre exists, hence no circle passes through three collinear points. Students conclude: a line cannot intersect a circle in three points.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the equidistance definition of a circle, this unit uses the perpendicular bisector as the locus of equidistant points — a connection worth naming explicitly. A common error is assuming the circumcentre always lies inside the triangle; emphasise that its position depends on the triangle's angle type, and this can be confirmed by construction with compass and ruler. For further independent reading, students may consult Exercise Set 5.1 Q2, p.98, which provides a concrete obtuse-triangle construction.
homework: Complete Exercise Set 5.1 Q1 and Q3, p.98: draw the specified triangles, construct the circumcircle, and state or measure where the circumcentre lies.

periods.activity_title: Equal Chords and the Angles They Subtend at the Centre

textbook_items_in_class.description: Show that the triangle formed by a chord and the centre of the circle is isosceles.
Show that two such isosceles triangles with equal base length are congruent to each other.

time_bands.activity: Draw a circle with centre O and two chords AB and CD of equal length. Ask students to draw the radii to each endpoint and measure the central angles AOB and COD. Record results from several students — all find equal central angles. State the conjecture as Theorem 2: equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre. Motivate the formal proof by asking: what triangle does a chord and two radii form?

Students work through Exercise Set 5.2 Q1, p.100 to confirm each chord-and-two-radii triangle is isosceles (since OA = OB = OC = OD as radii). Then Exercise Set 5.2 Q2, p.100: two such triangles with AB = CD have OA = OC (radii), OB = OD (radii), AB = CD (given), so the triangles are congruent by SSS, giving angle AOB = angle COD. This completes the proof of Theorem 2. Teacher formalises on the board.

Prove Theorem 3 (converse): chords subtending equal angles at the centre are equal. The two triangles now share two equal sides (radii) and an equal included angle, so congruence follows by SAS, giving AB = CD. Students write the argument in their own words, then compare with a partner.

Consolidation: the teacher poses a quick diagnostic — given two chords in a circle where one central angle is larger, which chord is longer? Students justify using Theorems 2 and 3. Record the converse relationship: longer chord ↔ larger central angle. Students note this chain will be revisited when distance from centre is introduced.

periods.teacher_notes: The isosceles-triangle structure (two radii as equal sides) is the hinge of every proof in this section — students who lose sight of it tend to attempt to use angle properties without first establishing the triangle. A common slip is applying SAS in Theorem 3 without checking that the equal angle is the INCLUDED angle between the two known equal sides; confirm this explicitly. Students comfortable with triangle congruence may read Think, Draw and Infer Q2, p.98 independently as it extends the circumcircle idea to congruent triangles.

periods.activity_title: Perpendicular from Centre Bisects a Chord — Theorems 4 and 5

textbook_items_in_class.description: Explain why the converse of Theorem 4 is true: the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
For isosceles triangle ABC inscribed in a circle with AB = AC, show that the altitude from A to BC passes through the centre.
Two parallel chords of lengths 6 cm and 8 cm lie on opposite sides of the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm; find the distance between the midpoints of the chords.

time_bands.activity: Draw a circle with centre O and chord AB. Drop the perpendicular from O to AB, meeting it at M. Ask: what can we say about AM and MB? Students measure on their own drawings and conjecture AM = MB. Present the proof of Theorem 4: triangles OAM and OBM share OM, have OA = OB (radii), and angle OMA = angle OMB = 90°, so they are congruent by RHS, giving AM = MB. Students write the proof step by step.

Exercise Set 5.3 Q1, p.101: students establish the converse (Theorem 5) — the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord — by reversing the argument and noting uniqueness of the foot of the perpendicular. Exercise Set 5.3 Q2, p.101: in an isosceles triangle inscribed in a circle, AB = AC means the altitude from A bisects BC perpendicularly; since the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre, the altitude from A passes through O.

Exercise Set 5.3 Q3, p.101: two parallel chords of lengths 6 cm and 8 cm on opposite sides of the centre, radius 5 cm. Students identify the perpendicular from O bisects each chord (half-lengths 3 and 4). Using the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem: distance from O to the 6 cm chord = √(25 − 9) = 4 cm; distance from O to the 8 cm chord = √(25 − 16) = 3 cm. Since the chords are on opposite sides, the distance between midpoints = 4 + 3 = 7 cm. Students present working.

Consolidate: students state in one sentence each what Theorem 4 asserts and what Theorem 5 adds. Teacher notes the two-way link: the centre's perpendicular to a chord meets it at its midpoint, and the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it — the same geometric fact read in two directions.

periods.teacher_notes: The isosceles-triangle congruence argument in Theorem 4 uses RHS; students sometimes apply SSS by treating OM as a third side without first checking that the right-angle condition is what makes the triangles congruent — insist that the right angle is named explicitly. A common error in Q3 is adding the two perpendicular distances without first checking which side of the centre each chord lies on; when chords are on opposite sides the distances add, not subtract. End-of-Chapter Q5, p.114 (Exercise E-26) provides a good independent proof task connecting perpendicular bisectors and the circumcentre result from Section 5.3.
homework: End of Chapter Q1, p.114 and End of Chapter Q9, p.114: apply the chord-distance formula to find the chord length and the radius respectively.

periods.activity_title: Distance of Chords from the Centre — Theorems 6 and 7

textbook_items_in_class.description: Use the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem to show why Theorem 6 must be true.
Given CE perpendicular to AB, CH perpendicular to GH, and CE = CH, show that AB = GF.
Solve the previous question using the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem.

time_bands.activity: Paper-folding and tracing-paper activity: students draw two equal chords AB and GF in a circle, fold to superimpose them, and observe that the perpendicular distances from the centre coincide. They trace one chord onto the other and measure. Use this as motivation for Theorem 6: equal chords are equidistant from the centre. Ask students to record the experimental finding before the formal proof begins.

Prove Theorem 6: drop perpendiculars from centre O to equal chords AB and GF. By Theorem 5, each perpendicular bisects its chord, giving half-lengths equal. In the right triangles formed, the hypotenuse (radius) is common and one leg (half-chord) is equal, so by RHS the triangles are congruent and the perpendicular distances are equal. Students formalise this in writing, then attempt Exercise Set 5.4 Q1, p.104 (Baudhayana-Pythagoras alternative: if r² = d² + (c/2)², equal c gives equal d).

Prove Theorem 7 (converse) via Exercise Set 5.4 Q2 and Q3, p.104: given equal perpendicular distances CE = CH, the right triangles have equal hypotenuse (radius) and equal leg (distance), so by RHS the half-chords are equal and hence the full chords are equal. Students work Q3 using the Baudhayana-Pythagoras route as an independent verification.

Quick application: teacher states two chords in a circle of radius 10 cm are at distances 6 cm and 8 cm from the centre respectively — are they equal? Students compute (chord lengths 16 and 12 respectively) and conclude they are not. Consolidate the equivalence: equal chord length ↔ equal distance from centre.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established Theorem 5 (perpendicular from centre bisects a chord), Theorem 6 now adds a distance-measurement layer; make sure students name the half-chord explicitly in their RHS triangles rather than working with the full chord length. A frequent error is using SSS instead of RHS by treating the full chord and the perpendicular as two sides without identifying the right angle. End-of-Chapter Q3, p.114 (E-24) and Q4, p.114 (E-25) offer self-study chord-distance problems students can attempt on their own.
homework: End of Chapter Q18, p.115: two parallel chords on the same side of the centre — set up and solve the simultaneous Baudhayana-Pythagoras equations to find the radius.

periods.activity_title: Longer Chord Lies Closer — Theorem 8 and Arc Definitions

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the length of a chord of a circle with radius 7 cm and perpendicular distance 6 cm from the centre.
Explain why the chord length formula 2 times square root of (r squared minus d squared) holds for perpendicular distance d and radius r.
Measure the angles subtended by arc AKB and arc CLD at centre O and state whether each is a minor or major arc.

time_bands.activity: Prove Theorem 8: of two unequal chords, the longer lies closer to the centre. Denote perpendicular distances d₁ and d₂ for chords of lengths c₁ > c₂. From the chord-distance formula r² = d² + (c/2)², a larger c forces a smaller d (since r is constant). Students work through the algebra and note the extreme cases mentioned in the chapter: the diameter has d = 0 (closest) and a chord shrinking to a point has d → r (furthest). Exercise Set 5.5 Q1, p.105: radius 7 cm, d = 6 cm; chord = 2√(49 − 36) = 2√13 cm. Q2, p.105: students derive and explain the formula.

Transition to Section 5.7. Define arc: any two points on a circle divide it into two arcs. Define minor arc (shorter) and major arc (longer), and the degenerate cases of a semicircle. Define the angle subtended by an arc at the centre as the central angle corresponding to the arc's sweep. Clarify that the same two endpoints give two arcs, one associated with the central angle swept through the minor arc and one with its reflex. Students draw examples and label arcs.

Exercise, p.107 (E-17): using the given figure, students measure the angles subtended by arc AKB and arc CLD at the centre O with a protractor and classify each as minor or major. Discuss: the central angle is the defining measure of the arc, so the two arcs from the same chord are supplementary (their central angles add to 360°). Students confirm this from their measurements.
Consolidation: students state the chord-distance formula and describe in one sentence how Theorem 8 follows from it. They also state the definition of minor and major arc in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Theorem 8 is the sharpest application of the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem — students sometimes misread the inequality direction, concluding that the longer chord is further away; the algebra r² = d² + (c/2)² makes the inverse relationship explicit and worth dwelling on. The note about the diameter being the chord closest to the centre (d = 0) is often surprising and worth making memorable. In Section 5.7 a common confusion is between the angle swept through the minor arc and the reflex angle swept through the major arc — confirm that both are well-defined but the chapter's convention at this stage uses the non-reflex angle unless stated otherwise.

periods.activity_title: Arc–Angle Theorem and the Semicircle Corollary — Theorem 9

textbook_items_in_class.description: In a circle with centre O, the central angle AOB is 60 degrees and the radius is 12 cm; find the length of chord AB.
An arc subtends 70 degrees at the centre; find the angle the arc subtends at a point on the circle.
AB is a diameter and C is on the circumference; find the measure of angle ACB and explain the reasoning.

time_bands.activity: State Theorem 9: the angle an arc subtends at the centre is double the angle it subtends at any point on the circle outside the arc. Present Case 1 (centre inside the angle): join the point on the circle to the centre, extending to the opposite arc. The two smaller triangles formed are isosceles (radii). Using the exterior-angle property of each isosceles triangle, students derive that the central angle = 2 × the inscribed angle. Teacher works through Case 2 (centre outside the angle) with students, applying the same exterior-angle property.

Derive the semicircle corollary: when the arc is a semicircle, the central angle is 180°, so the inscribed angle is 90°. End of Chapter Q6, p.114 (E-27): AB is a diameter, C is on the circumference; students state angle ACB = 90° and write the reasoning chain. End of Chapter Q2, p.114 (E-23): arc subtends 70° at centre; angle at circumference = 35°. Students present both solutions.

Establish that angles subtended by the same arc at different points on the circle (all outside the arc) are equal — a direct consequence of Theorem 9 (each equals half the fixed central angle). Exercise Set 5.6 Q1, p.110 (E-18): central angle 60°, radius 12 cm; triangle AOB is isosceles and equilateral (since angle AOB = 60° and OA = OB), so chord AB = 12 cm. Students verify this with a construction.

Exercise Set 5.6 Q3, p.111 (E-20): find x in the given cyclic-angle configuration with one given angle of 100°. Students apply Theorem 9 to determine the central angle, then find x. Confirm by symmetry of the diagram.

periods.teacher_notes: The two-case proof of Theorem 9 is where students most often stumble: they apply the exterior-angle property to the wrong triangle or forget to account for the case where the centre is outside the inscribed angle. Make both cases visible simultaneously on the board. A frequent error in the semicircle corollary is concluding that any inscribed angle in a circle is 90° rather than specifically those subtended by a diameter; stress the 'arc is a semicircle' condition. Exercise Set 5.6 Q2, p.111 (E-19) is a rich independent investigation of equal inscribed angles and concyclicity that students may read on their own.
homework: End of Chapter Q20, p.115: MNOP inscribed in a circle with MN a diameter — determine and explain angles MOP and MNP using Theorem 9.

periods.activity_title: Concyclic Points and Cyclic Quadrilateral Angle Theorems

textbook_items_in_class.description: A cyclic quadrilateral has angles A = 80 degrees, B = 110 degrees, C = 100 degrees, D = 70 degrees; determine whether such a quadrilateral can be drawn and explain why.
ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle A = 75 degrees; find angle C, and with angle B = 110 degrees, find angle D.
Quadrilateral PQRS is inscribed in a circle with angle P = (2x+10) degrees and angle R = (3x-20) degrees; find x and the measures of angle P and angle R.
For cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, explain why the exterior angle at any vertex equals the interior opposite angle.

time_bands.activity: State and prove Theorem 10: if a segment AB subtends equal angles at two points C and D on the same side, then A, B, C, D are concyclic. The proof proceeds by contradiction: assume the circle through A, B, C does not pass through D; then D lies inside or outside the circle, but in either case the angle ADB cannot equal angle ACB — a contradiction with the hypothesis. Students follow the argument step by step and identify what is assumed and what is contradicted.

Define cyclic quadrilateral. Prove Theorem 11: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°. Using the central-angle result of Theorem 9: each pair of opposite vertices subtends arcs that together form the full circle (360°), so the inscribed angles sum to 180°. Students draw a cyclic quadrilateral, label the arcs, and write the proof. Exercise, p.113 (E-21): angles 80°, 110°, 100°, 70°; check 80° + 100° = 180° ✓ but 110° + 70° = 180° ✓; total = 360° ✓ — yes, this quadrilateral can be cyclic. Students explain why.

End of Chapter Q7, p.114 (E-28): angle A = 75°, find angle C = 105°; angle B = 110°, find angle D = 70°. End of Chapter Q8, p.114 (E-29): (2x + 10) + (3x − 20) = 180, so 5x − 10 = 180, x = 38; angle P = 86°, angle R = 94°. Students work independently, teacher circulates. End of Chapter Q21, p.115 (E-34): exterior angle at vertex D = 180° − angle D = angle B, the interior opposite angle, following from Theorem 11.

Prove Theorem 12 (converse of Theorem 11) by contradiction: if the sum of a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral is 180°, the quadrilateral is cyclic. Assume it is not cyclic; then one vertex lies off the circumcircle of the other three; but the angle at that vertex would then not satisfy the 180° sum condition — a contradiction. Students identify the key step in the contradiction. Close by having students state all three theorems of Section 5.8 in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The proof of Theorem 10 by contradiction is the first extended use of proof by contradiction in this chapter; students may conflate it with direct proof and need to be reminded that the contradiction is with the hypothesis, not with some other fact. A common error in Theorem 11 calculations is using the wrong pair of opposite angles (confusing adjacent with opposite); confirming which vertices are opposite in a labelled diagram helps. End of Chapter Q26, p.116 (E-36) is an excellent self-study item in which students justify Theorem 11 using the central-angle diagram of Theorem 9.
homework: End of Chapter Q10, p.114 and End of Chapter Q26, p.116: the first asks for the area of a cyclic kite using the semicircle corollary, and the second asks students to justify the opposite-angle sum result from the central-angle diagram.

assessment_items.subject: mathematics
assessment_items.chapter_title: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can state the locus definition of a circle and identify radius, chord, and diameter in a given figure, justifying why the diameter is the longest chord.
questions.section_context: locus definition of circle; radius, chord, diameter terminology

competency.competency_text: Chord, subtended-angle, and inscribed-polygon properties of circles.

questions.question_text: A line segment PQ is drawn inside a circle with centre O such that P and Q are both on the circle. Which of the following statements correctly describes PQ and explains why the diameter is the longest such segment?

options.label: A
options.text: PQ is a chord; the diameter is the longest chord because it is the only chord that is also a line of symmetry of the circle.

options.label: B
options.text: PQ is a chord; the diameter is the longest chord because it passes through the centre, making each half a radius — the maximum possible distance from the centre to the circle — so the total length 2r cannot be exceeded by any chord.

options.label: C
options.text: PQ is a diameter; every segment joining two points on a circle passes through the centre.

options.label: D
options.text: PQ is a radius; the diameter is the longest radius because it connects two points on the circle.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses 'chord' with 'radius' — the student has not distinguished a segment joining two circle points from one joining the centre to a circle point.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Correctly identifies PQ as a chord but gives an incorrect reason for the diameter's maximality — conflating the symmetry property with the length property; a chord can be a line of symmetry only if it is a diameter, but this does not explain why 2r is the maximum length.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates 'chord' with 'diameter' — assumes every segment connecting two circle points must pass through the centre, which contradicts the definition of a chord.

MCQ.inclusivity: A student who is uncertain may first mark P, Q, and O on a diagram and measure PQ versus a diameter to build the intuition. A student ready for extension may be asked to prove formally, using the triangle inequality applied to the triangle OPQ, that OP + OQ ≥ PQ and hence 2r ≥ PQ.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can justify why every diameter is a line of reflection symmetry and why a circle has complete rotational symmetry about its centre, using the equidistance definition.
questions.section_context: reflection symmetry across diameters; complete rotational symmetry of circle

competency.competency_text: Chord, subtended-angle, and inscribed-polygon properties of circles.

questions.question_text: A student claims: 'A circle has exactly two lines of reflection symmetry — the horizontal diameter and the vertical diameter — because only these two directions split the circle into identical halves.' Using the definition of a circle as a locus of points equidistant from its centre, identify the flaw in this claim and write a correct, justified statement about the reflection symmetries of a circle.
look_for: States that the student's claim is wrong because it restricts symmetry to two specific diameters without justification.
Uses the locus definition: every point on the circle is at distance r from the centre O.

Argues that any diameter divides the plane into two half-planes and that reflecting a point P on the circle across the diameter maps it to a point P' at the same distance r from O on the opposite side, so P' also lies on the circle.

Concludes that every diameter is a line of reflection symmetry, and since infinitely many diameters exist (one for each direction through O), the circle has infinitely many lines of reflection symmetry.
Optionally notes that rotational symmetry by any angle about O is also a symmetry for the same equidistance reason.

ECR.inclusivity: A student who struggles may be invited to fold a physical paper circle along three different diameters to observe that each fold produces coinciding halves, then express this observation in words using the vocabulary 'equidistant' and 'centre'. A student who engages confidently may be challenged to extend the argument: explain why a regular hexagon has exactly 6 lines of symmetry while a circle has infinitely many, identifying what changes as the number of sides grows without bound.

questions.question_text: Two points A and B are marked on a page. (a) Explain, with a geometric justification, how many circles can pass through A and B, and describe where the centres of all such circles must lie. (b) A third point C is added such that A, B, C are not collinear. Prove that exactly one circle passes through A, B, and C, and identify the centre of this circle.
look_for: Part (a): States that infinitely many circles pass through A and B.
Part (a): Correctly identifies that the centre of any such circle must be equidistant from A and B, hence must lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
Part (b): Notes that the centre of the circle through A, B, C must lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB and also on the perpendicular bisector of BC.
Part (b): Argues that the two perpendicular bisectors of two sides of a non-degenerate triangle are not parallel and meet at exactly one point — the circumcentre.
Part (b): Concludes that this unique point is equidistant from A, B, and C, so exactly one circle (the circumcircle) passes through all three points.
Optionally notes that if A, B, C were collinear the two perpendicular bisectors would be parallel and no such circle would exist.

ECR.inclusivity: A student who finds the abstract argument difficult may be guided to first draw the perpendicular bisector of AB with a compass and ruler, mark several centres on it, draw the corresponding circles, and observe that all pass through A and B — then extend this drawing step to locate the circumcentre for part (b). A student ready for a challenge may be asked additionally to state and justify where the circumcentre of a right-angled triangle lies (on the hypotenuse, at its midpoint) and connect this to the smallest possible radius for a circle through A and B.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can determine whether the circumcentre of a triangle lies inside, on, or outside the triangle based on its angle type.

competency.competency_text: Chord, subtended-angle, and inscribed-polygon properties of circles.

questions.question_text: Triangle PQR has angle P = 115°. Where does the circumcentre of triangle PQR lie?

options.label: A
options.text: At the vertex P, because P has the largest angle and is therefore closest to the centre.

options.label: B
options.text: Inside the triangle, because the triangle has one large angle.

options.label: C
options.text: On the side QR, at its midpoint, because the longest side is opposite the largest angle.

options.label: D
options.text: Outside the triangle, on the opposite side of QR from P, because triangle PQR is obtuse.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the position rule — the student knows the circumcentre is inside for acute triangles but incorrectly applies that case here because angle P = 115° makes the triangle obtuse.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates the circumcentre with the midpoint of the hypotenuse, which is the correct location only for a right triangle; the student has over-generalised the right-triangle rule.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Invents a non-existent rule linking the largest angle to the circumcentre's position; the circumcentre is determined by perpendicular bisectors, not by angular proximity.

MCQ.inclusivity: A student who is uncertain may construct the circumcentre for a specific obtuse triangle (e.g., angles 30°, 35°, 115°) with compass and ruler to observe directly that it falls outside. A student seeking a challenge may be asked to explain why the circumcentre of a right triangle lies exactly at the midpoint of the hypotenuse, connecting this to the semicircle corollary proved later in the chapter.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can prove that equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre (Theorem 2) and its converse (Theorem 3) using SSS and SAS triangle congruence.

questions.question_text: Circle with centre O has two chords AB and CD. (a) Given AB = CD, prove that angle AOB = angle COD. (b) Given angle AOB = angle COD, prove that AB = CD. In each part, state the congruence criterion you use and explain why it applies.
look_for: Part (a): Sets up triangles OAB and OCD.
Part (a): States OA = OC = OB = OD (all radii of the same circle).
Part (a): Notes AB = CD (given), so all three sides of the triangles are equal — applies SSS congruence.
Part (a): Concludes angle AOB = angle COD as corresponding angles in congruent triangles.
Part (b): Sets up the same two triangles with OA = OC, OB = OD (radii) and angle AOB = angle COD (given).
Part (b): Identifies the equal angle as the included angle between the two pairs of equal sides — applies SAS congruence.
Part (b): Concludes AB = CD as the corresponding third sides.
Explicitly names the congruence criterion used in each part and states it is applicable by checking the conditions.

ECR.inclusivity: A student who struggles to start may be invited to draw the two triangles separately, label all sides with r or the chord length, and decide which sides and angles match — converting the abstract proof into a labelled diagram step. A student working confidently may be asked to explain whether the same argument works for chords in two different circles of the same radius, and whether the proof requires both circles to be the same circle or just congruent.

questions.question_text: A circle has centre O and radius 10 cm. Two parallel chords PQ and RS are drawn on opposite sides of O with lengths 12 cm and 16 cm respectively. Find the perpendicular distance between the midpoints of PQ and RS, showing all working.
questions.method_one_line: Apply Theorem 5 to find that O's perpendicular to each chord bisects it; use the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem in each right triangle to find the perpendicular distance from O to each chord, then add the two distances since the chords are on opposite sides of O.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who is uncertain may be guided to draw the diagram, mark the foot of each perpendicular from O to the chords (the midpoints), and label the right triangles before setting up the Pythagoras equation. A student who solves this quickly may be asked: if the two chords were on the same side of O, how would the calculation change, and what would the distance between midpoints be?

questions.question_text: Circle with centre O has chords AB and CD. Let OE be perpendicular to AB at E, and OF be perpendicular to CD at F. (a) Given AB = CD, prove that OE = OF. (b) State what additional conclusion you can draw if you are instead given OE = OF, and prove it.
look_for: Part (a): States that OE bisects AB (Theorem 5) and OF bisects CD (Theorem 5), so AE = AB/2 and CF = CD/2.
Part (a): Since AB = CD, we have AE = CF.
Part (a): In right triangles OEA and OFC: hypotenuse OA = OC (radii), leg AE = CF; by RHS the triangles are congruent.
Part (a): Concludes OE = OF as corresponding sides.
Part (a): Alternatively accepts: r² = OE² + AE² = OF² + CF²; since AE = CF and r is the same, OE = OF.
Part (b): States the conclusion is AB = CD (Theorem 7 — the converse).
Part (b): In right triangles OEA and OFC: OA = OC (radii), OE = OF (given), angle OEA = angle OFC = 90°; by RHS the triangles are congruent.
Part (b): Concludes AE = CF, hence AB = 2AE = 2CF = CD.

ECR.inclusivity: A student who is unsure may be reminded to first invoke Theorem 5 to establish the bisection, which reduces each chord to a known half-length in the right triangle, making the RHS criterion visible. A student who finishes quickly may be asked to re-derive both results using the Baudhayana-Pythagoras equation r² = d² + (c/2)² directly, confirming that both proof routes yield the same conclusion.

questions.question_text: A circle has radius 13 cm. Chord AB is at a perpendicular distance of 5 cm from the centre, and chord CD is at a perpendicular distance of 12 cm from the centre. Find the lengths of AB and CD, and state which chord is longer and which lies closer to the centre.
questions.expected_answer: AB = 24 cm, CD = 10 cm; AB is longer and lies closer to the centre (d = 5 cm < 12 cm).
questions.method_one_line: Apply the chord-length formula chord = 2√(r² − d²) separately for each chord, then compare lengths and distances to confirm Theorem 8.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who is uncertain may be guided to draw each right triangle (half-chord, distance, radius as the three sides) and label r, d, and c/2 before substituting into Pythagoras. A student who completes this readily may be asked: as d increases from 0 to r, describe what happens to the chord length and what the chord becomes when d = r.

questions.question_text: Points X and Y lie on a circle with centre O, and the central angle XOY (measured through the minor arc) is 110°. What is the central angle subtended by the major arc XY at O, and what type of arc is the major arc?

options.label: A
options.text: 70°; the major arc subtends the angle that is the complement of the minor arc's angle.

options.label: B
options.text: 110°; both arcs subtend the same central angle because they share the same endpoints.

options.label: C
options.text: 180°; the two central angles are supplementary because they form a straight line.

options.label: D
options.text: 250°; the major arc is the longer arc from X to Y.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the two distinct central angles associated with the same chord — the student has not recognised that the minor and major arcs are swept by different angles (110° and 250° respectively) even though both are bounded by X and Y.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Applies the supplementary-angles rule (180°) rather than the full-revolution rule (360°) — the student treats the two arcs as if their central angles form a linear pair rather than together completing a full rotation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Subtracts from 90° rather than 360° — the student has confused 'complement' with 'the remaining angle after going around the full circle', producing 70° instead of 250°.

MCQ.inclusivity: A student who is unsure may draw a circle, mark X and Y, shade the minor arc in one colour and the major arc in another, and measure or calculate both central angles to confirm they sum to 360°. A student who answers quickly may be asked: if the minor arc's central angle were exactly 180°, what would both arcs be called, and what would the chord XY be?

questions.question_text: Circle with centre O has points A, B on the circle and a third point P on the major arc (so P is outside the minor arc AB). (a) Prove that angle AOB = 2 × angle APB, for the case where O lies inside angle APB. (b) Use this theorem to prove that if AB is a diameter, then angle APB = 90°.
look_for: Part (a): Draws line PO extended to meet the circle at a point Q on the opposite side.
Part (a): Identifies triangles OPA and OPB as isosceles (OA = OP = OB = radius).
Part (a): Uses the exterior-angle theorem on triangle OPA: angle AOQ = angle OPA + angle OAP = 2 × angle OPA (since OA = OP, base angles are equal).
Part (a): Similarly angle BOQ = 2 × angle OPB.
Part (a): Adds: angle AOB = angle AOQ + angle BOQ = 2(angle OPA + angle OPB) = 2 × angle APB.
Part (b): States that if AB is a diameter, the central angle AOB = 180° (a straight angle).
Part (b): Applies Theorem 9: angle APB = angle AOB / 2 = 90°.
Clear logical sequence with all steps justified by named properties.

ECR.inclusivity: A student who finds the abstract setup difficult may first draw the diagram with specific values (e.g., angle APB = 40°, then measure angle AOB) to verify the 2:1 ratio numerically before writing the proof. A student working confidently may be asked to write the proof for Case 2 (where O lies outside angle APB) and explain why the exterior-angle step changes but the conclusion does not.

questions.question_text: In a circle with centre O, points A, B, C, and D all lie on the circle. The central angle AOB = 84°. Point C lies on the major arc AB (outside the minor arc), and point D also lies on the major arc AB. Find angle ACB and angle ADB, showing your working and stating the theorem used at each step.
questions.method_one_line: Apply Theorem 9: each inscribed angle equals half the central angle on the same arc; since C and D are both on the major arc, both inscribed angles equal 84°/2 = 42°.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who is uncertain may mark C and D at two clearly different positions on the major arc, draw in the four relevant radii, and measure the inscribed angles to observe they are equal before applying the theorem algebraically. A student who finishes quickly may be asked: if E were placed on the minor arc instead of the major arc, what would angle AEB be, and why does it differ from 42°?

questions.task: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle with centre O. You are given that angle A = (3y − 10)° and angle C = (y + 30)°, and that angle B = 95°. (a) Use the property of cyclic quadrilaterals to write and solve an equation for y, then find the measures of all four angles of ABCD. (b) A student claims that any quadrilateral whose opposite angles sum to 180° must be cyclic. Explain whether this claim is correct, stating the relevant theorem and the direction of proof it relies on.
questions.scaffold: For part (a): which pairs of angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are related? Set up one equation from that relationship and solve for y, then find the remaining angle using the same or another relationship. For part (b): consider whether the theorem you used in part (a) has a converse, and what would need to be proved for the converse to hold.
format_of_output: Written working for the equation and solution in part (a)
All four angle values clearly stated
A written argument in part (b) naming the theorem and its converse

OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The task requires building an algebraic equation from the cyclic-quadrilateral angle property and solving it, then evaluating a claim about the converse — combining the computational and proof-evaluation dimensions of the section's two implied LOs within a single coherent scenario.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can apply Theorem 11 to set up and solve a linear equation for an unknown angle, and whether the student can identify and articulate Theorem 12 as the converse that validates the claim in part (b).
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students to identify the 'opposite angle' relationship first — this is the key step that converts the geometric situation into an equation. Students who are unsure which angles are opposite in ABCD should be encouraged to label the vertices on a diagram before writing any algebra.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: sets up (3y − 10) + (y + 30) = 180 correctly, solves y = 40, states all four angles (A = 110°, C = 70°, B = 95°, D = 85°), and in part (b) names Theorem 12 explicitly, stating it is the converse of Theorem 11 proved by contradiction. Weak: uses 95° + angle D = 180° but makes an arithmetic error; or in part (b) simply says 'yes it is cyclic' without naming or justifying the converse.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: A student who struggles with part (b) may be guided to re-read the statement of Theorem 12 in the chapter and identify which direction of implication it proves. A student who completes the task confidently may be asked to construct a numerical counterexample that appears to satisfy the angle-sum condition but fails concyclicity — or explain why no such counterexample can exist given Theorem 12.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can prove Theorem 12 (converse of Theorem 11) by contradiction and justify properties of cyclic quadrilaterals including the exterior-angle result.

questions.question_text: Quadrilateral PQRS has angle P + angle R = 180°. A student wants to conclude that PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral. Outline a proof by contradiction that establishes this conclusion, identifying clearly what is assumed, what known theorem is applied, and where the contradiction arises.
look_for: Clearly states the assumption for contradiction: PQRS is NOT a cyclic quadrilateral.
Considers the circle through P, Q, R and notes that S does not lie on this circle — so S lies strictly inside or strictly outside it.

For the case S lies inside: the point S' on the circle on the same side as S satisfies angle P + angle RS'Q = 180° (by Theorem 11 applied to PQS'R); since S is inside the circle, angle PSQ > angle PS'Q (as the inscribed angle from inside is larger than from the circle), so angle P + angle PSQ > 180° — contradiction with the given angle P + angle R = 180° where angle R = angle PSQ.
States (or handles symmetrically) the case where S lies outside the circle, obtaining the reverse inequality and the same type of contradiction.
Concludes that the assumption is false, so PQRS must be cyclic.
The argument is logically sequenced and names Theorem 11 as the source of the 180° relationship for the circumscribed quadrilateral PQS'R.

ECR.inclusivity: A student who finds proof by contradiction unfamiliar may be guided to first write down the structure: 'Assume … Then … But … Contradiction' as a template, then fill in each slot for this specific situation. A student who completes the proof may be challenged to write the exterior-angle result for a cyclic quadrilateral (that the exterior angle at any vertex equals the interior opposite angle) as a corollary of Theorem 11, and prove it in two lines.
